climate_pressure: Higher temperatures, declining precipitation and drought; projected dry-season water decline.
documented_impact: Water shortage, unreliable public supply and costly private alternatives.
fcv_mediator: Unequal access, affordability, service failure, perceived unfairness and pre-existing group/resource competition.
possible_consequence: Where governance and distribution are already contested, additional water stress could worsen grievances or intergroup tensions.
geographies: strongest directly observed perception evidence in Beirut/Mount Lebanon and Beirut/Beqaa tension analysis
uncertainty: No source reviewed estimates an independent causal effect of climate change on violent conflict.
compact_statement: Climate-related water stress may aggravate tension through service failure and perceived inequity, but scarcity alone is not demonstrated to cause conflict. (World Bank)

documented_impact: Self-reported livelihood/financial losses, especially among rural and economically precarious respondents.
fcv_mediator: Informal employment dependence, reduced household income, competition over jobs/resources and existing economic crisis.
possible_consequence: Climate-sensitive livelihood shocks could intensify competition and social tension where labour markets and household finances are already stressed.
affected_groups: displaced Syrians working in climate-sensitive sectors
uncertainty: Survey respondents attribute losses to climate; causal attribution was not independently tested.
compact_statement: Climate-sensitive livelihood losses may compound job/resource competition, but political economy and labour-market conditions remain independent drivers.

climate_pressure: Heat, drought, floods and other climate hazards remain external pressures.
documented_impact: Crisis-constrained public finances and conflict-damaged lifeline infrastructure.
fcv_mediator: Reduced fiscal space, maintenance failures, implementation constraints and reconstruction burdens.
possible_consequence: Climate hazards may produce larger service and welfare impacts because institutions and infrastructure have less capacity to absorb shocks.
geographies: especially conflict-damaged South/Nabatiyeh and service-stressed urban areas
alternative_explanations: Long-standing infrastructure underinvestment and governance weaknesses predate recent hostilities
uncertainty: Sources demonstrate damage and capacity constraints more directly than they measure resulting changes in climate vulnerability.
resilience_factors: protected maintenance finance and NAP integration
compact_statement: The strongest reverse pathway is that conflict and economic collapse weaken infrastructure and institutions needed to manage climate risk. (World Bank)

climate_pressure: Drought/heat and water stress may affect agriculture and livelihoods.
fcv_mediator: Conflict, displacement, loss of purchasing power and reduced humanitarian assistance.
possible_consequence: Additional climate-related production or income shocks could compound food insecurity and competition for scarce assistance or employment.
geographies: with rural and displacement-affected areas potentially more exposed
alternative_explanations: The cited 2025 evidence explicitly identifies conflict
displacement and reduced assistance - not climate - as the main immediate food-insecurity drivers
uncertainty: No reviewed source apportions the 2025 IPC burden quantitatively to climate.
compact_statement: Climate shocks could compound food insecurity, but the recent acute burden cannot be credibly described as climate-driven.

documented_impact: Water access can become a focus of local stress and mistrust.
fcv_mediator: Service-provider accountability, communication and intercommunity dialogue.
possible_consequence: Well-designed WASH investment may reduce tension while strengthening capacity to manage climate-related water stress.
geographies: candidate nationally only as a programme theory
alternative_explanations: Dialogue or wider political changes may have contributed independently
uncertainty: No counterfactual evaluation; the observed local experience does not establish general effectiveness.
compact_statement: WASH projects can potentially serve as peace-supporting adaptation when infrastructure and dialogue are deliberately combined.

climate_pressure: Increasing water scarcity/drought can add stress to already contested resources.
documented_impact: Local competition over springs/groundwater and high reliance on informal/private provision.
fcv_mediator: Ambiguous land/water rights, weak enforcement, fragmented governance and perceived unequal allocation.
possible_consequence: Under worsening scarcity, unresolved institutional disputes could become harder to mediate and reduce cooperation needed for adaptation.
alternative_explanations: sectarian politics and governance failures can generate conflict independent of climatic change
uncertainty: Climate's contribution to the specific Bcharreh-Denniyeh conflict is not isolated.
compact_statement: Climate stress may amplify contested water governance, but the causal core of documented local disputes is institutional and political as well as environmental.

climate_pressure: Water, heat or energy-related resilience needs can motivate geographically targeted investment.
documented_impact: Independent LHSP evaluation found that uneven infrastructure/solar support sometimes created intermunicipal grievances.
fcv_mediator: Beneficiary selection, geographic targeting, transparency and perceived distributive fairness.
possible_consequence: Climate/adaptation investments could unintentionally intensify local grievances if benefits are visibly unequal and conflict sensitivity is weak.
geographies: Evaluation examples from Akkar and Bekaa
uncertainty: LHSP was not a climate-adaptation programme, so transfer to climate programming is an explicitly cautious inference.
compact_statement: Adaptation finance itself can become conflict-sensitive when allocation is unequal; evaluated Lebanese development experience provides a concrete warning.
